title: Quantum electrodynamics: how electrons and photons interact
text: Quantum electrodynamics is the theory of how electrons, positrons, and photons exchange energy and momentum. Everything else in that theory is a way of calculating those exchanges.

support.source: QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter; Nobel lecture, 1965

title: Path integrals: every possible path carries a little arrow
text: Each way an event can happen carries a little arrow, an amplitude. Add the arrows for the ways you cannot tell apart, and the probability is the square of the resulting length.
aliases: how does the path integral work

title: A Feynman diagram is not a picture of a trajectory
text: A Feynman diagram writes a term in the calculation. The lines are not a movie of where the particle went, and the horizontal direction is not a clock on the wall.
aliases: how to read a Feynman diagram

title: An antiparticle is an electron running backward in time
text: With Stueckelberg, he read a positron as an electron moving backward in time. It is a way to keep one kind of line in the diagram and still count both particles.
aliases: why is the positron an electron going backward in time

title: Renormalization is not sweeping infinities under the rug
text: Self-energy and vacuum polarization make the raw integrals infinite. Renormalization absorbs those infinities into the measured mass and charge, and what is left is a number you can check.

title: The electron g factor is not exactly 2
text: Dirac's equation gives the electron a magnetic moment of two Bohr magnetons. The real electron sits a little off 2, and the shift is one of the successes of the higher-order QED calculation.
aliases: why is the electron moment not 2

title: Vacuum polarization and the Lamb shift
text: The vacuum is not a blank. Virtual pairs screen a charge, and that screening shows up in the Lamb shift and in vacuum polarization.

title: The force between two electrons is virtual-photon exchange
text: In the theory, two electrons push on each other by exchanging photons. The exchanged photon is off the mass shell; it is a term in the amplitude, not a free flash of light.
aliases: where does the Coulomb force come from

title: 1/137 makes QED work, and makes it fail in strong fields
text: The fine-structure constant is about 1/137, so each extra meeting of a photon with a charge is a small factor. That is why the series works in ordinary fields, and why it is the wrong tool when the field is enormous.

title: The photon has no rest mass, and that is why c is the limit
text: A photon with a rest mass would make the Coulomb force die off with distance and would make the speed of light depend on color. The mass is zero, and c is the limit the kinematics enforce.
aliases: why is the speed of light the limit

title: Nuclear force comes from meson exchange, but that is not the whole strong force
text: Yukawa's 1935 picture of the nuclear force as meson exchange gets the range roughly right. It is not the whole strong interaction, which at short distance is quarks and gluons.
aliases: where does the nuclear force come from

title: Partons: hitting a proton with electrons hits nearly free points
text: In deep inelastic scattering a fast electron hits the proton and bounces as if it had struck something small and nearly free. He called those pieces partons.

title: Asymptotic freedom and confinement are two ends of one coupling
text: The strong coupling gets smaller as the energy goes up, which is why partons look free in a hard collision, and it gets large as the energy goes down, which is why you never see a lone quark.
aliases: why can't a quark exist alone

support.source: later QCD, set against his parton picture

title: The weak force: slow, short-ranged, and able to change particle type
text: Beta decay is the weak interaction: slow, very short-ranged, and able to change one kind of particle into another.

title: Parity violation: the bet Feynman lost
text: In 1956 Lee and Yang said the weak interaction might not respect mirror symmetry. The experiment showed it did not. Feynman had bet the other way, and he said so.

support.source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!; Lee and Yang, 1956

title: Neutrinos barely interact with anything
text: A neutrino feels only the weak force, so it goes through almost anything. The ones made in the Sun stream out of the Sun, and out of the Earth, with almost no collisions.
aliases: why are neutrinos hard to detect

title: Electroweak unification is one framework, not one sentence
text: Above the scale of the heavy bosons, electromagnetism and the weak force are one gauge theory, SU(2) times U(1). That is a framework, not a single sentence you can say in the kitchen.
aliases: are electromagnetism and the weak force the same

support.source: electroweak theory as he discussed it in later lectures

title: The Higgs boson, found in 2012
text: The Higgs boson was found at CERN in 2012. It supplies masses in the gauge theory worked out in the 1960s and 1970s. That discovery is later knowledge. It is not a result from his papers, and it is not something to put in his mouth.
aliases: did Feynman know about the Higgs

support.note: Model-learned modern knowledge, not a passage from Feynman's corpus. The Higgs boson was announced by CERN in 2012. That discovery is not a result from his papers.

title: Conservation laws come from symmetry
text: In Volume III, chapter 17, every conservation law is tied to a symmetry: if the description can be shifted without changing the predictions, something is conserved.

title: The field is fundamental; particles are excitations of it
text: He did not treat the field as a messenger running between solid particles. The field is the thing, and the particle is an excitation of it.

title: Superconductivity is more than zero resistance
text: A superconductor does more than lose its resistance. Below the transition it pushes magnetic field out of its bulk, the Meissner effect.
aliases: is zero resistance the same as superconductivity

title: Cooper pairs and the energy gap
text: Electrons in a superconductor pair, very weakly, through the lattice. The pair has a gap to the next state, and that gap is why the flow does not scatter.
aliases: why does a superconductor have no resistance

support.source: BCS theory as presented in his lectures

title: The Josephson effect makes a macroscopic phase measurable
text: Two superconductors separated by a thin barrier let pairs tunnel. The current depends on the phase difference across the barrier, so a macroscopic quantum phase becomes something you can measure.

support.source: Josephson effect, as discussed in his later lectures

title: Superfluid helium: a quantum liquid with no viscosity
text: Below 2.17 K, liquid helium-4 flows with no viscosity you can measure. He treated it as a quantum liquid, not as an ordinary fluid that happens to be slippery.
aliases: why does liquid helium climb walls

support.source: his papers on liquid helium; FLP

title: Band structure decides conductors, insulators and semiconductors
text: In a crystal the electrons may sit only in allowed bands, with gaps between. A filled band cannot carry a current; a partly filled band can. That is the difference between insulator and metal.

title: A pn junction: one side has electrons, the other holes
text: Dope one side of a semiconductor with acceptors and you have holes; dope the other with donors and you have extra electrons. The junction between them is the diode.
aliases: how does a pn junction work
why does a diode conduct one way

title: Phonons are quantized lattice vibrations
text: The atoms in a lattice are always shaking. Quantize a normal mode of that shake and you have a phonon, the sound quantum.
aliases: how does heat travel through a solid

title: Only electrons near the Fermi surface conduct
text: In a metal the electrons fill every state up to the Fermi energy. Only the ones at the top of that sea can take a small kick and move. The ones deep inside have nowhere to go.
aliases: why is the electronic specific heat small

title: The partition function is the door to every thermodynamic quantity
text: At temperature T a state of energy E is weighted by e to the minus E over kT. The sum of those weights is the partition function, and the thermodynamic quantities are derivatives of its logarithm.

support.source: FLP I-40 and the statistical mechanics lectures

title: The three statistics differ on whether particles may share a state
text: Classical distinguishable particles follow Maxwell-Boltzmann counting. Fermions refuse to share a state. Bosons prefer to. The three counting rules are the whole difference.

title: A phase transition is an order parameter appearing or vanishing
text: In a phase transition an order parameter appears or disappears, and some symmetry of the hotter phase is lost or restored.

title: The Ising model: the simplest phase transition
text: The Ising model is the smallest phase transition: spins that are only up or down, coupled to their neighbors. It is a toy, and it already freezes.

title: Entropy is the logarithm of the number of microscopic states
text: Entropy is k times the log of the number of microscopic states that look the same from outside. 'Disorder' is a metaphor for that count, and two different messes can have the same entropy.

title: Brownian motion is direct evidence of atoms
text: A speck in a liquid jitters because the molecular kicks do not cancel. Brownian motion is evidence you can see that matter is made of atoms.
aliases: how do we know atoms exist

title: A ratchet cannot run on a single heat bath
text: A ratchet and pawl in one heat bath cannot turn noise into steady rotation. The pawl has a temperature too, and it slips.
aliases: why can't a ratchet do work

title: A plasma is a shielded collective gas
text: In a plasma each charge gathers a cloud of the opposite sign. Beyond the shielding length the bare Coulomb force is hidden.

support.source: FLP I, plasma discussions in the kinetic theory chapters

title: A laser runs on stimulated emission and population inversion
text: A photon of the right frequency, hitting an atom already excited, makes the atom emit another photon in step with the first. A laser needs that stimulated emission, and a population that is upside down so emission wins over absorption.

support.source: FLP III and his laser remarks

title: The refractive index does not come from light being dragged
text: Light is not dragged to a lower speed by sticky atoms. The wave that comes out of the medium is the incident wave plus the waves the driven charges radiate, and the sum lags.
aliases: where does the refractive index come from
why does light slow in glass

title: Least time and diffraction are the same story
text: Reflection, refraction, and diffraction are one rule: the amplitude is large where neighboring paths take nearly the same time, and it cancels where the time changes quickly from path to path.
aliases: why does light take the shortest time

title: A single photon either gets through or it doesn't: polarization as a two-state system
text: A polarizer does not peel a classical vector into a piece that passes and a piece that stops, not for one photon. The photon goes through or it does not, with a probability set by the angle, as a two-state system.
aliases: how does a single photon get through a polarizer
what is the polarization state of a photon

title: Light and electrons are neither classical waves nor classical particles
text: Light and electrons are neither classical waves nor classical pellets. They are described by amplitudes. Interference is the adding of those amplitudes.
aliases: is light a wave or a particle

title: Equivalence principle: gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable
text: Inside a closed elevator you cannot tell a gravitational field from an acceleration. That local indistinguishability is the equivalence principle, and it is where he starts gravitation.

support.source: The Character of Physical Law; his lectures on gravitation

title: Gravitational waves really carry energy: the sticky bead
text: Put beads that can slide, with a little friction, on a rod. A passing gravitational wave shakes the rod and the beads rub. The heat in the beads is energy the wave carried.

title: The horizon is where escape velocity reaches the speed of light
text: The Schwarzschild radius is 2GM/c². Inside it, the escape speed reaches c, so no signal gets out. Light sent inward does not come back.

title: The universe expands without galaxies flying through space
text: The redshift of a distant galaxy is not the galaxy flying through a fixed space. The scale of the space itself is growing, and the wavelength grows with it.
aliases: what does it mean that the universe expands

support.source: FLP I, the cosmology remarks; standard FLRW reading he used

title: There is plenty of room at the bottom: thinking at the nanometer
text: In 1959 he asked what happens if the whole Encyclopaedia Britannica is written small enough to sit on a pinhead, and then what happens if we arrange atoms one by one.
aliases: plenty of room at the bottom

support.source: There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom, 1959

title: Quantum simulation: use nature to simulate nature
text: A classical computer simulating a quantum system has to keep every amplitude. He argued in 1982 for using a quantum system to simulate a quantum system.

title: Erasing one bit costs kT ln 2 of heat
text: Erasing one bit of information dissipates at least kT ln 2. Computation is physical. Forgetting is a thermodynamic act.
aliases: why does erasing information produce heat

title: A rainbow's colours come from dispersion: water bends different colours differently
text: A raindrop bends different colors by different amounts, because the index of water depends on wavelength. That spread of angles is the rainbow.
aliases: why is blue bent more than red

title: A rainbow is not seven blocks of colour: the spectrum is continuous
text: A prism or a raindrop spreads sunlight into a continuous band. The seven named colors are a way of talking, not seven blocks sitting in the spectrum.
aliases: why is a rainbow always seven colours
why does a rainbow have seven colours
where do the seven colours come from
which seven colours are in the rainbow

title: Light bends at a surface by taking the quickest path
text: Light going from air into glass bends. The rule underneath the ray is that the path taken is the one that makes the travel time least.
aliases: what is the law of refraction
what is the principle of least time
why does light bend in water

title: The sky is blue because air scatters blue light more
text: Air molecules are driven by the electric field of sunlight and radiate again in all directions. The scattered power goes as the fourth power of the frequency, so blue is scattered far more than red, and the sky looks blue.
aliases: why is the sky blue and sunsets red

title: A lens focuses light by the least time, again
text: A lens is another least-time device. He does not start from a memorized ray diagram. He compares travel times along neighboring paths and asks where they agree.
aliases: how does a lens form an image
why does a magnifying glass focus light

title: Synchrotron radiation: light squeezed into a narrow cone
text: A charge whipped around a circle near the speed of light does not radiate evenly. The light is thrown forward into a narrow cone. That is synchrotron radiation.
aliases: why do electrons radiate in a magnetic field
why does the Crab nebula glow

title: Colour is in the eye, not the light: three-colour mixing and night vision
text: One sensation of color can be made by many different spectra. What the eye reports is how its three pigments were driven, not the spectrum itself. At night the color machinery drops out.
aliases: why can't we see colour in the dark
why does the eye have three kinds of cone

title: The eye is a piece of brain touching light
text: The eye is a piece of brain that is touching light, so to speak, on the outside. The retina is not a passive window; a lot of the processing happens before the signal leaves the eye.
aliases: how does the eye form an image
why is a compound eye resolution limited

support.quote: The eye is a piece of brain that is touching light, so to speak, on the outside.

title: Interference: add the fields of the two sources first, then square
text: For two sources, add the electric fields first and square afterward. Squaring first throws away the interference.
aliases: what is constructive and destructive interference
why do two waves cancel each other
how can two antennas beam a signal in one direction
why can't intensities simply be added

title: Diffraction: the superposition of many sources
text: He opens the diffraction chapter by saying nobody has ever cleanly separated interference from diffraction; it is a matter of usage. With many sources the pattern is what we call diffraction.
aliases: how does a diffraction grating work
what is the difference between interference and diffraction
what limits the resolution of a telescope
why is the edge of a shadow not sharp

support.quote: No one has ever been able to define the difference between interference and diffraction satisfactorily.

title: Polarization: the electric field of light is a vector, and it matters which way it vibrates
text: The electric field of a light wave points across the direction of travel. Which way it points is the polarization, and polarizers and reflection care about that direction.

title: Dielectric polarization: the charges in an insulator are pulled apart a little
text: In an insulator the charges are tied to their atoms. An applied field pulls plus and minus a little apart. That slight separation is the dielectric polarization.
aliases: why does a capacitor store more charge with a dielectric
